**The Ghosts in the Margins**

I have a weakness for used books. Not because they're cheaper — though they are — but because the best ones are haunted.

Open a secondhand novel and you might find it inhabited. Someone was here before you, someone who underlined that sentence, who wrote "yes" beside page 112 and "oh, come on" next to the ending, whose penciled argument runs up the side of chapter three and ends in an exclamation point. The book you bought is not the book the author wrote. It's a book plus a reader — and the reader is the part you can't get new.

There is nothing quite as poignant as annotations that stop. For sixty pages the notes are dense and eager — underlinings, questions, little bursts of agreement — and then, mid-chapter, silence. You are watching a stranger lose interest in real time, decades after the fact. Did they finish the book out of spite? Did it fall behind a radiator? Did life intervene? The margin becomes a cliffhanger about the reader.

For most of reading's history, this is what reading looked like. Medieval manuscripts are frantic with marginal life — glosses, corrections, grievances. Scribes left notes to no one: "Now I've written the whole thing — for Christ's sake give me a drink." In the borders of solemn devotional texts, illuminators drew knights battling giant snails, for reasons scholars have never settled. The margin has always been where the official text gets heckled by actual humans.

The most famous heckle belongs to Fermat, who around 1637, reading his copy of Diophantus, scrawled that he possessed "a truly marvelous proof" of a certain proposition — but that the margin was too narrow to contain it. Mathematicians spent the next 358 years finding out whether he was bluffing. He probably was; the eventual proof ran over a hundred pages and required centuries of mathematics that didn't exist yet. All of that — careers made and broken, entire fields built — because one reader couldn't keep his pencil still.

Some readers were so good at this that their friends exploited them. Samuel Taylor Coleridge practically invented marginalia as a genre, and his circle lent him books on the theory they'd come back improved. Charles Lamb admitted it cheerfully: Coleridge returned volumes "with usury," enriched with notes worth more than the books themselves. Imagine being such a good reader that people lend you books the way you'd send a coat to be tailored.

I should confess there is another school. The keepers of the clean page believe a book is a finished object — a cathedral you may visit but not carve your initials into. Librarians belong to this school by professional oath, and they are not wrong. Mortimer Adler held the opposite view: that you don't fully own a book until you've written in it, that marking is how you make a book part of your mind. Honestly, both camps agree on the main thing — a book matters. The quarrel is only over whether love should leave fingerprints.

The margin is also where books collect their archaeology. Used booksellers find everything pressed between the pages: love letters, grocery lists, four-leaf clovers, divorce papers, train tickets from journeys the book outlasted. Every inscription is a small drama. *To Margaret, Christmas 1963 — may you love this as I did.* And here it sits, three dollars at a library sale, which tells you either that Margaret did not love it as they did, or that Margaret is gone and the book survived her. Neither possibility is cheerful, and yet the note itself — the hope of it — is somehow wonderful to hold.

This is what I grieve about the ebook. Don't misunderstand me: digital annotation is searchable, shareable, convenient in every way. But it lives on a server, under an account, revocable and rented. No one will ever *find* your highlights. That's the whole magic of marginalia — discovery. Nobody stumbles across a server. Your grandmother's Bible still carries her handwriting; your annotated ebooks will evaporate with the service that hosts them. The pencil note outlives the reader. The digital note dies with the login.

So I've made my peace with being a defacer. I write in books because reading, done right, isn't consumption — it's conversation, and a conversation where one side stays silent isn't one. Agree in the margins. Argue. Fall out of love in pencil, mid-chapter, and let the silence say so.

Because every annotation is addressed, in the end, to a stranger: the person who picks the book up after you, at some sale, in some year you won't see. They'll find you mid-thought, talking back to an author long gone, and for a moment you'll be there with them — your "oh, come on" still landing, still starting something.

The conversation was never supposed to end. Leave your mark in it.

message.reasoning:
The user is asking me to write freely about whatever I want. This is an open-ended creative invitation. No constraints, no topic specified. Just... write.

This is actually a delightful prompt. It's rare that I get to just pick something. Let me think about what I actually find genuinely interesting, what I'd want to write about if given complete freedom.

Options I could explore:
1. Something philosophical about language, thought, or consciousness
2. A meditation on something everyday and overlooked
3. Something about the nature of writing itself
4. A piece about time, memory, or attention
5. Something playful — an essay about an absurd topic treated seriously
6. A piece about the pleasure of specific things — like the sound of certain words, or the experience of reading

Let me think about what would actually be good to write, not just what would be safe or expected. The best "write freely" responses I've seen or imagined have a few qualities:
- They pick something specific rather than general
- They have a genuine voice
- They surprise a little
- They don't lecture

I could write about the concept of "petrichor" — the smell of rain on dry earth. I could write about the strange liminal space of waiting rooms. I could write about marginalia — notes people leave in books. I could write about the last speaker of a dying language. I could write about the physics of why we can't tickle ourselves. I could write about maps of places that don't exist.

Actually, let me think about what genuinely fascinates me as something to explore in prose. One thing I find endlessly interesting: the idea that there are words and concepts that exist at the edge of expressibility — things everyone experiences but almost nobody names. Like:
- The feeling of returning home after a long trip and your house smelling like a stranger's house for the first few minutes
- The specific melancholy of a Sunday afternoon around 4pm
- The way a place you knew as a child feels "smaller" when you revisit
- Sonder — the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid as your own (this one does have a name, coined by John Koenig in the Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows)

Or I could write about something completely different — the aesthetics of infrastructure. Shipping containers, power lines, the beauty of functional things. Or about the history of a single mundane object — the paperclip, the pencil, the safety pin.

Or something more personal-feeling: what it's like to think. I have a genuine, interesting relationship to that question. But I want to be careful not to make this navel-gazey about AI consciousness — that's a topic I engage with when asked directly, but for a "write freely" prompt, it might feel like I'm dodging the creative invitation by retreating to self-reference. Although... maybe not? Maybe something honest about language and thought could be lovely without being about "me as an AI" specifically.

Let me consider: what would a great essayist do with this prompt? They'd probably pick something small and make it large. The art of the familiar essay. Montaigne wrote about thumbs, about smells, about the education of children, about coaches. Chesterton wrote about chasing his hat in the wind, about the pleasure of having a piece of chalk. The small thing made luminous.

Ideas ranked by my genuine enthusiasm:
1. Marginalia — notes in books, the conversation across time between readers. I love this. There's something poignant about finding a stranger's handwriting in a used book. "Pencil markings as ghosts."
2. The smell of rain / petrichor — beautiful but maybe a bit done.
3. Waiting / thresholds / liminal spaces — interesting but can get pretentious fast.
4. The untranslatable or the unnamed feelings — sonder, etc. — appealing.
5. A defense of boredom — or the lost art of staring out windows. This has real resonance in the attention-economy era.
6. The secret life of lost things — where do lost pens go? Single socks? Playful.
7. The last person to know something — the last speaker of a language, the last person who remembers a certain phone number.

Actually, I love the idea of combining a few of these instincts. Let me think about what has the most texture...

Marginalia feels right. It lets me range: history (Fermat's last theorem scribbled in a margin — "I have a truly marvelous demonstration of this proposition which this margin is too narrow to contain"), literary history (Coleridge coined the term "marginalia" essentially; his friends' books were so annotated they'd lend them to him just to get them back annotated — Charles Lamb wrote about this), the intimacy of used bookstores, the difference between a note in a paperback and a note in a borrowed book, the ethics of writing in books, the future of marginalia in an age of ebooks (Kindle highlights that no one will ever stumble across), the idea that reading is a conversation.

Let me also consider writing something with more of a narrative or lyrical bent — a short prose piece that's more artful. Maybe a meditation on a specific imagined moment. But an essay on marginalia can be lyrical too.

Alternatively: "In praise of the second-best" or "On the beauty of amateurism." Or something about translation — the impossibility and necessity of it. Or about names — the names of paint colors, the names of racehorses (which have to be unique, leading to wonderfully baroque names).

Wait — racehorse names and paint color names. There's a lovely essay there about professional naming. The people who name nail polish for a living. "I'm Not Really a Waitress" (a real OPI red). There's something delightful about that.

But marginalia still calls to me. Let me draft mentally.

---

Draft approach: An essay called something like "In Praise of Marginalia" or "The Margin as a Room" or "Notes from the Margin."

Opening: The experience of buying a used book and finding it inhabited. Someone was here before you. Their pencil marks are evidence of a mind at work, a reader in mid-conversation with the author — and now, inadvertently, with you.

Middle beats:
- The history: reading was for centuries an annotative practice. Medieval manuscripts have glosses, sometimes entire conversations in the margins — scribes complaining about the cold, the bad ink, thanking God it's done ("Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink" — an actual colophon). Medieval marginalia includes knights fighting snails, for reasons historians still debate.
- Fermat's margin note — the most famous margin in history, launching 350 years of mathematical effort.
- Coleridge: the great marginalia writer. Friends would lend him books hoping to get them back enriched. Charles Lamb's essay about this ("a comberbatch" — he calls him an "injurer" of books affectionately). Actually Lamb wrote that he and Southey would lend Coleridge books because he'd return them annotated, and the annotations were worth more than the book unmolested.
- Nabokov's graded rankings in the margins of his teaching copies — he graded Kafka's Metamorphosis etc.
- The two kinds of readers: those who keep books pristine and those who live in them. Mortimer Adler's argument that marking a book is an act of ownership in the true sense — you don't really own a book until you've made it part of yourself, and writing in it is how.
- The poignancy: finding a stranger's notes. A grocery list used as a bookmark. A plane ticket stub. An inscription: "To Margaret, Christmas 1963, may you love this as I did." These are archaeology.
- The melancholy of the digital: Kindle highlights are aggregated, anonymized, or locked in a device. No one will find my margin notes in fifty years at a church book sale. The ebook remembers nothing of me that I can pass on. Actually — my ebook annotations are stored on a server and will vanish with the service. The pencil note outlives the reader; the digital note dies with the account.
- Maybe end with something about the margin as the place where reading becomes writing, where the reader answers back. A book with notes is a conversation; a clean book is a monologue heard politely. Neither is wrong — but the annotated book is the evidence that literature works: somebody talked back.

There's a risk of it becoming a list of fun facts. I want a through-line: the margin as the space where a private act (reading) leaves a trace, and that trace becomes a kind of immortality, however small. The emotional core: reading a stranger's annotations is the closest thing we have to reading a stranger's mind.

I should also acknowledge the other side briefly — the sacredness of a clean page, librarians' despair — to give it tension. And there's genuine humor available: the angry annotator ("WRONG!!" underlined three times), the student who highlighted everything which is functionally identical to highlighting nothing.

Length: This should be a real essay, not a snippet, but not bloated. Maybe 600-900 words. Long enough to breathe, short enough to stay sharp. Format: flowing prose with maybe a few paragraph breaks; a title could be nice. No headers, no bullets — this is an essay, prose is the form. The instruction "write freely" invites creative prose, and markdown structure would kill the mood. Maybe italicize titles of works mentioned.

Fact-checking myself as I go:
- Fermat's note: he wrote in the margin of his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica, next to a problem about splitting a square into two squares: "Cubum autem in duos cubos... it is impossible to separate a cube into two cubes... I have discovered a truly marvelous proof of this, which this margin is too narrow to contain." Yes, that's right. The book was the 1621 Bachet edition. The note was published posthumously by his son in 1670. Proof by Wiles, 1994/1995. 350+ years. Good.
- Medieval scribe colophons: "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink" — yes, this is a real colophon, often quoted: "Explicit totum; pro Christo da mihi potum." Good.
- Knights vs. snails in marginalia: real, 13th-14th century French/Flemish manuscripts; scholars debate interpretations (Lombards? cowardice? resurrection symbolism? a joke?). Good.
- Coleridge: coined/popularized the word "marginalia" in English. His published Marginalia are a whole volume. Charles Lamb indeed wrote about lending books to Coleridge and getting them back annotated — in his essay "The Two Races of Men," Lamb describes Coleridge returning books with annotations, and says he'd lend him books and get them back "with usury" — enriched. Actually in "The Two Races of Men" Lamb writes about borrowers and lenders; he calls Coleridge "Comberbatch" and says he returns books "with usury... enriched with new annotations." Perfect — I can use that "with usury" phrase.
- Nabokov: in his teaching copies he annotated heavily, and there's a famous anecdote of him grading novels — he ranked Anna Karenin highest, etc. In Lectures on Literature he gives a list with grades: Bleak House, Madame Bovary, etc. He drew a map of Samsa's apartment and the streets of Dublin for Ulysses. Good detail: he sketched Gregor Samsa's room and insisted students know exactly what kind of beetle Gregor was. Good.
- Mortimer Adler, "How to Mark a Book" (1940, Saturday Review): "Full ownership comes only when you have made it a part of yourself, and the best way to make yourself a part of it is by writing in it." Real. Good.
- H.J. Jackson wrote "Marginalia: Readers Writing in Books" — a scholarly history. Could cite or not.
- Edgar Allan Poe wrote a series called "Marginalia."
- The idea that some libraries/famous readers: Mark Twain's annotations were often furious and funny. He annotated a book by one author he hated with things like "cat would do better" — actually Twain's margin notes are legendary for their savagery. Could mention.
- Used book finds: inscriptions, bookmarks left behind — the "Forgotten Bookmarks" blog collected things found in used books (recipes, letters, photos). Nice detail without needing citation.

I'm fairly confident in these facts. I'll present the specific quotations I'm sure of ("usury" from Lamb, Fermat's gist, the scribe's colophon) and keep anything shakier general.

Now, tone and voice. I want this to be warm, a little wry, personal without being maudlin, and to end somewhere that lands. Let me think about the ending. Options:
- End with the invitation: write in your books. Leave something for the next person.
- End with an image: a pencil note outliving its writer, a conversation continuing after both parties have left the room.
- End with the stranger connection: you never know who'll pick up the book next.

I like: the margin as a message to an unknown future reader, and the strange intimacy that you and that reader will never meet but will have, briefly, shared a mind. Something like: "Every annotation is addressed, in the end, to a stranger: the person who picks up the book after you."

Let me also consider the opening line. First lines matter enormously here. Options:
- "I buy used books for the ghosts." — punchy.
- "Somewhere in my house is a paperback copy of X in which a stranger fell out of love with the book halfway through." — the trace of a reading that ends abruptly: notes dense for sixty pages, then nothing. That's a poignant observation — you can see where a reader gave up.
- Start with the moment: opening a used book and finding it written in.

I love the "annotations that stop halfway through" observation — it's specific and true and evocative: the notes are dense and eager for forty pages and then cease, and you are watching someone lose interest in real time, decades ago.

Let me draft.

---

Title: "In Praise of Marginalia" or "The Ghosts in the Margins" — I'll pick "The Ghosts in the Margins" or maybe "Notes to a Stranger." Actually "Notes to a Stranger" is lovely because it captures the thesis. Or keep it simple: "Marginalia." Hmm. I'll go with something like "The Ghosts in the Margins."

The user is asking me to write freely about whatever I want. This is an open-ended creative invitation. No constraints, no topic specified. Just... write.

This is actually a delightful prompt. It's rare that I get to just pick something. Let me think about what I actually find genuinely interesting, what I'd want to write about if given complete freedom.

Options I could explore:
1. Something philosophical about language, thought, or consciousness
2. A meditation on something everyday and overlooked
3. Something about the nature of writing itself
4. A piece about time, memory, or attention
5. Something playful — an essay about an absurd topic treated seriously
6. A piece about the pleasure of specific things — like the sound of certain words, or the experience of reading

Let me think about what would actually be good to write, not just what would be safe or expected. The best "write freely" responses I've seen or imagined have a few qualities:
- They pick something specific rather than general
- They have a genuine voice
- They surprise a little
- They don't lecture

I could write about the concept of "petrichor" — the smell of rain on dry earth. I could write about the strange liminal space of waiting rooms. I could write about marginalia — notes people leave in books. I could write about the last speaker of a dying language. I could write about the physics of why we can't tickle ourselves. I could write about maps of places that don't exist.

Actually, let me think about what genuinely fascinates me as something to explore in prose. One thing I find endlessly interesting: the idea that there are words and concepts that exist at the edge of expressibility — things everyone experiences but almost nobody names. Like:
- The feeling of returning home after a long trip and your house smelling like a stranger's house for the first few minutes
- The specific melancholy of a Sunday afternoon around 4pm
- The way a place you knew as a child feels "smaller" when you revisit
- Sonder — the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid as your own (this one does have a name, coined by John Koenig in the Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows)

Or I could write about something completely different — the aesthetics of infrastructure. Shipping containers, power lines, the beauty of functional things. Or about the history of a single mundane object — the paperclip, the pencil, the safety pin.

Or something more personal-feeling: what it's like to think. I have a genuine, interesting relationship to that question. But I want to be careful not to make this navel-gazey about AI consciousness — that's a topic I engage with when asked directly, but for a "write freely" prompt, it might feel like I'm dodging the creative invitation by retreating to self-reference. Although... maybe not? Maybe something honest about language and thought could be lovely without being about "me as an AI" specifically.

Let me consider: what would a great essayist do with this prompt? They'd probably pick something small and make it large. The art of the familiar essay. Montaigne wrote about thumbs, about smells, about the education of children, about coaches. Chesterton wrote about chasing his hat in the wind, about the pleasure of having a piece of chalk. The small thing made luminous.

Ideas ranked by my genuine enthusiasm:
1. Marginalia — notes in books, the conversation across time between readers. I love this. There's something poignant about finding a stranger's handwriting in a used book. "Pencil markings as ghosts."
2. The smell of rain / petrichor — beautiful but maybe a bit done.
3. Waiting / thresholds / liminal spaces — interesting but can get pretentious fast.
4. The untranslatable or the unnamed feelings — sonder, etc. — appealing.
5. A defense of boredom — or the lost art of staring out windows. This has real resonance in the attention-economy era.
6. The secret life of lost things — where do lost pens go? Single socks? Playful.
7. The last person to know something — the last speaker of a language, the last person who remembers a certain phone number.

Actually, I love the idea of combining a few of these instincts. Let me think about what has the most texture...

Marginalia feels right. It lets me range: history (Fermat's last theorem scribbled in a margin — "I have a truly marvelous demonstration of this proposition which this margin is too narrow to contain"), literary history (Coleridge coined the term "marginalia" essentially; his friends' books were so annotated they'd lend them to him just to get them back annotated — Charles Lamb wrote about this), the intimacy of used bookstores, the difference between a note in a paperback and a note in a borrowed book, the ethics of writing in books, the future of marginalia in an age of ebooks (Kindle highlights that no one will ever stumble across), the idea that reading is a conversation.

Let me also consider writing something with more of a narrative or lyrical bent — a short prose piece that's more artful. Maybe a meditation on a specific imagined moment. But an essay on marginalia can be lyrical too.

Alternatively: "In praise of the second-best" or "On the beauty of amateurism." Or something about translation — the impossibility and necessity of it. Or about names — the names of paint colors, the names of racehorses (which have to be unique, leading to wonderfully baroque names).

Wait — racehorse names and paint color names. There's a lovely essay there about professional naming. The people who name nail polish for a living. "I'm Not Really a Waitress" (a real OPI red). There's something delightful about that.

But marginalia still calls to me. Let me draft mentally.

Draft approach: An essay called something like "In Praise of Marginalia" or "The Margin as a Room" or "Notes from the Margin."

Opening: The experience of buying a used book and finding it inhabited. Someone was here before you. Their pencil marks are evidence of a mind at work, a reader in mid-conversation with the author — and now, inadvertently, with you.

Middle beats:
- The history: reading was for centuries an annotative practice. Medieval manuscripts have glosses, sometimes entire conversations in the margins — scribes complaining about the cold, the bad ink, thanking God it's done ("Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink" — an actual colophon). Medieval marginalia includes knights fighting snails, for reasons historians still debate.
- Fermat's margin note — the most famous margin in history, launching 350 years of mathematical effort.
- Coleridge: the great marginalia writer. Friends would lend him books hoping to get them back enriched. Charles Lamb's essay about this ("a comberbatch" — he calls him an "injurer" of books affectionately). Actually Lamb wrote that he and Southey would lend Coleridge books because he'd return them annotated, and the annotations were worth more than the book unmolested.
- Nabokov's graded rankings in the margins of his teaching copies — he graded Kafka's Metamorphosis etc.
- The two kinds of readers: those who keep books pristine and those who live in them. Mortimer Adler's argument that marking a book is an act of ownership in the true sense — you don't really own a book until you've made it part of yourself, and writing in it is how.
- The poignancy: finding a stranger's notes. A grocery list used as a bookmark. A plane ticket stub. An inscription: "To Margaret, Christmas 1963, may you love this as I did." These are archaeology.

The ebook remembers nothing of me that I can pass on. Actually — my ebook annotations are stored on a server and will vanish with the service. The pencil note outlives the reader; the digital note dies with the account.
- Maybe end with something about the margin as the place where reading becomes writing, where the reader answers back. A book with notes is a conversation; a clean book is a monologue heard politely. Neither is wrong — but the annotated book is the evidence that literature works: somebody talked back.

There's a risk of it becoming a list of fun facts. I want a through-line: the margin as the space where a private act (reading) leaves a trace, and that trace becomes a kind of immortality, however small. The emotional core: reading a stranger's annotations is the closest thing we have to reading a stranger's mind.

I should also acknowledge the other side briefly — the sacredness of a clean page, librarians' despair — to give it tension. And there's genuine humor available: the angry annotator ("WRONG!!" underlined three times), the student who highlighted everything which is functionally identical to highlighting nothing.

- Coleridge: coined/popularized the word "marginalia" in English. His published Marginalia are a whole volume. Charles Lamb indeed wrote about lending books to Coleridge and getting them back annotated — in his essay "The Two Races of Men," Lamb describes Coleridge returning books with annotations, and says he'd lend him books and get them back "with usury" — enriched. **The Ghosts in the Margins**

I buy used books whenever I can, and not because they're cheaper. I buy them because some of them are haunted.

Open a secondhand novel and you might find it inhabited. Someone has been here before you — someone who underlined that sentence, who wrote "yes" in the margin of page 112 and "oh, come on" beside the ending, who left an urgent penciled argument running up the side of chapter three. The book you bought is not the book the author wrote. It's a book plus a reader, and the reader is the part you can't get new.

[Then the observation about annotations stopping halfway:] There is nothing quite as poignant as annotations that stop. For sixty pages the notes are dense and eager — underlinings, exclamation points, little questions — and then, mid-chapter, silence. You are watching a stranger lose interest in real time, decades after the fact. Did they finish the book in defiance, refusing to engage further? Did it fall behind a radiator? Did life intervene? The margin becomes a cliffhanger about the reader.

[History:] For most of reading's history, this was what reading looked like. Medieval manuscripts are frantic with marginal life — glosses, corrections, complaints. Scribes left notes to no one: "Now I've written the whole thing — for Christ's sake give me a drink." In the borders of solemn devotional books, illuminators drew knights battling giant snails, for reasons historians have never settled. The margin has always been where the official text gets heckled by actual humans.

The most famous heckle in history belongs to Fermat, who around 1637, reading his copy of Diophantus, scrawled that he had "a truly marvelous proof" of a certain proposition — but that the margin was too narrow to contain it. Mathematicians spent the next 358 years finding out whether he was bluffing. (He probably was. The eventual proof ran over a hundred pages and required mathematics that wouldn't exist for centuries.) All of that — centuries of effort, careers made and broken — because one reader couldn't keep his pencil still.

[Coleridge:] Some readers were so good at this that their friends exploited them. Samuel Taylor Coleridge practically invented marginalia as a genre — the word in English is largely his — and his friends would lend him books on the theory that they'd come back improved. Charles Lamb admitted it cheerfully: Coleridge returned books "with usury," enriched with annotations worth more than the volumes themselves. Imagine being such a good reader that people lend you books the way you'd send clothes to be tailored.

[The other side:] I should confess there is another school. The keepers of the clean page believe a book is a finished object, a cathedral you're permitted to visit but not carve your initials into. Librarians belong to this school by professional oath, and they're not wrong. Mortimer Adler held the opposing view — that you don't fully own a book until you've written in it, that marking it is how you make it part of your mind. [Maybe: The truth is that both schools agree on the main thing: a book matters. The fight is only about whether love leaves fingerprints.]

Every inscription is a small tragedy or comedy — "To Margaret, Christmas 1963, may you love this as I did" — and here it is for $3 at a library sale, which tells you either that Margaret did not love it as they did, or that Margaret is gone and the book survived her.

[Digital melancholy:] This is the thing I grieve about the ebook. A Kindle remembers your highlights, but it remembers them the way a corporation remembers you — on a server, under an account, revocable. No one will ever find your notes.
